# Ratana Sutta (Snp 2.1 (PTS Snp 39))

**ID:** Snp 2.1 (PTS Snp 39)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Ratana Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ratana Sutta* ("Gems" or "Discourse on the Precious") is the opening discourse of the Cūḷavagga in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 2.1) and is duplicated as the sixth text of the *Khuddakapāṭha* (Kp 6) [DharmaNexus; Anālayo 2018; Rahula 1978]. The text celebrates the supreme treasures of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha—dedicating seven of its stanzas specifically to the virtues of the Saṅgha, including the "Eight Persons" and "Four Pairs" [Rahula 1978]. Opening by addressing terrestrial and celestial spirits gathered together, the verses appeal to benevolent non-human entities and invoke protective truth-utterances (*saccavacana*) [Gombrich 1991]. According to commentarial tradition, the discourse was taught in connection with a disaster at Vesālī, when the Buddha instructed Ānanda to recite the text and sprinkle holy water from his bowl throughout the city [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Adikaram 1946].

Alongside the *Maṅgala Sutta* and the *Mettā Sutta*, the *Ratana Sutta* forms a triad of the most frequently chanted and memorized texts in Theravāda practice [Anālayo 2018; Gombrich 1991]. It opens the standard paritta collection (*Catubhānavāra*), where it is ranked among the foremost protective recitations (*paritta*) used to ward off misfortunes, expel malignant spirits, and cure pestilence [Gombrich 1991; Rahula 1956; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Early commentarial sources record that ancient teachers debated its composition, with some holding that only the first five verses were spoken directly by the Buddha while others ascribed the entirety to him [Adikaram 1946]. In medieval Sri Lankan history, King Sena II reportedly had the text inscribed upon a plate of gold to receive offerings [Gombrich 1991].

 Furthermore, the complete *Ratana Sutta* is embedded within the Sanskrit *Mahāsāhasrapramardana-sūtra* [Holz], matching Tibetan translations such as D0558, D0813, and D4407 (*Vaiśālīpraveśasvastigāthā*) as confirmed by DharmaNexus [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, beyond its full identity with Kp 6, passages are reused in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.4, Kv 2.2) [DharmaNexus].
